About

Personal statement

I am a Research Scientist at the University of Texas at Austin, where my work centers on the molecular mechanisms by which transcription factors regulate chromatin structure and gene expression. Building on my earlier tenure as a Staff Scientist at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI), I bring a broad background in protein biochemistry, structural biology, and chromatin regulation, with specific expertise in transcription factor–nucleosome interactions and histone modification dynamics.

My recent collaborative research revealed that the bHLH transcription factor SCREAM (SCRM) functions as a pioneer-like factor, engaging nucleosomes and promoting chromatin remodeling. My contributions include the structural and biochemical dissection of this mechanism — cryo-EM and NMR analysis, protein–nucleosome binding assays, and histone methyltransferase studies.

Over more than two decades I have published upward of 50 peer-reviewed articles, including recent work in Science Advances, Nature Communications, Nature Plants, and PNAS, and I have solved and deposited fourteen structures in the Protein Data Bank. I have extensive experience mentoring students and postdoctoral researchers and leading multidisciplinary collaborations.

My combination of hands-on structural biology, quantitative biophysics, and mechanistic chromatin biology positions me to deliver transformative insight into transcription-factor–mediated chromatin regulation — from plant developmental reprogramming to chemokine-driven inflammation.

Education: Ph.D., Biochemistry & Biophysics · Osmania University, Hyderabad, India. Postdoctoral training, National Tsing Hua University, Taiwan.

Research program

Themes & project backgrounds

Four interconnected research lines, each grounded in structural and biophysical mechanism.

Flagship · Chromatin & development

bHLH transcription factors in cell-fate control

How do developmental transcription factors gain access to their targets within chromatin? Working with structural and plant-developmental biologists, I helped define how the master basic helix–loop–helix (bHLH) regulator SCREAM (SCRM) partners with SPCH, MUTE, and FAMA to govern the successive asymmetric and symmetric divisions of the stomatal lineage.

Through chemical-genetic and structural approaches, this work identified small molecules that perturb stomatal differentiation and established a framework with broad implications for chromatin-associated gene regulation in plants and other eukaryotes.

Key papers: Sci Adv 2025 · Nat Commun 2024 · Nature Plants 2022 · PNAS 2022
Immunology · Structural biophysics

Chemokine plasticity, glycosaminoglycans & neutrophil trafficking

Using solution NMR, ITC, SPR, and analytical ultracentrifugation, I defined how ELR⁺ CXC chemokines (CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL8, CXCL5) use structural plasticity to fine-tune neutrophil recruitment. I established that glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) do more than concentrate chemokines — they actively remodel chemokine architecture into distinct monomer, dimer, and heterodimer states with unique signaling outputs.

I reported the first structural basis for a chemokine heterodimer (CXCL1–CXCL2) binding GAGs and showed it is a more potent neutrophil chemoattractant than either homodimer — establishing heterodimerization as a physiologically relevant tuning mechanism for CXCR2 signaling in inflamed tissue.

Key papers: J Leukoc Biol 2023 · Biochem J 2021 · iScience 2020 · J Biol Chem 2016–2019
Biophysics · Cancer signaling

Non-classical secretion: S100 proteins, FGF & RAGE

I dissected the protein–protein assemblies that drive the non-classical (ER/Golgi-independent) secretion of acidic fibroblast growth factor (FGF1) and interleukin-1α. I solved structures of the S100A13-containing multiprotein complexes and characterized S100 family interactions with the RAGE receptor, and designed fragment-based inhibitors targeting cancer-inducing FGFs (FGF1/FGF2) for lung cancer therapy.

Key papers: J Biol Chem 2010–2011 · Biochemistry 2010–2012 · Biochim Biophys Acta 2014
Molecular pathogenesis

How intracellular pathogens manipulate their host

I characterized RC0497, a zinc-dependent peptidoglycan amidase and novel virulence factor from Rickettsia conorii, and defined the structural basis by which the Ehrlichia chaffeensis nucleomodulin TRP120 uses intrinsically disordered tandem repeats and a coupled folding-binding mechanism to recognize GC-rich promoters and reprogram host transcription.

Key papers: Biol Chem 2020 · PLoS One 2018 · Int J Mol Sci 2022
